items.question: What is the nature of the self, its bondage, and its liberation?

It appears bound due to the concealment of its own splendor.

This, in summary, is the varied meaning manifested here for the varied form of reality.

items.question: How does false knowledge obscure reality and how is that obscuration removed?
premises: False knowledge is an unequaled darkness that produces defects of vision.
Because of it, even the pure appears as an abode of impurity.
When true vision removes the seal of defect caused by darkness, suspicion of impurity cannot arise.
items.inference: False knowledge distorts perception, making the pure seem impure; true vision removes this distortion, eliminating any doubt about purity.

items.question: Why is calling the dynamic reality insentient considered a misunderstanding?
premises: The multitude of beings forcibly seizes people's hearts and makes them dance, concealing the heart of the self.
Anyone who calls this dynamic reality insentient is themselves insentient and badly taught.
Calling such a person insentient is actually a word of praise, as it suggests a similarity to that dynamic reality.
items.inference: The dynamic play of reality is not insentient; those who fail to recognize its conscious play are themselves insentient, and ironically, that insentience mirrors the very dynamism they deny.
uncertainties: The exact parsing of 'bhāvavrāta?' as a vocative is inferred from context; the text shows a question mark in the source.
items.plain_english: O multitude of beings, having forcibly seized people's hearts and making them dance with various gestures, you play while concealing the heart of the self. Whoever calls you insentient is himself insentient, badly taught in the belief that he has a heart. I think that calling him insentient is actually a word of praise, because it suggests a similarity to you.
